# What happens when you type in VS Code?

This is a recorded investigation of **desktop VS Code 1.137.0
(Electron)**. The generator launches a separate profile and empty workspace;
it never attaches to an existing user window. Commands use PowerShell quoting.
The IDs, paths, and source URLs below are the actual values from that run.
Use the identities discovered on your own machine when following along.

## Discover, select, and inspect

Find the isolated process tree. When following along manually, omit the filter
to discover your own windows, then select a renderer PID from that output.

````console
$ dbgjs process list --root vscode --no-cmd-line --filter p:33216
VS Code process tree 33216  (6 attachable processes; window metadata available)
└─ p:33216  Code.exe  [vscode-main]
   ├─ w:33216/1  window  readme-demo - Visual Studio Code
   │  ├─ p:10904  extension-host  [extension-host]
````

Create a durable context, attach to that renderer, and evaluate inside it.

````console
$ dbgjs context create :readme 'VS Code typing' --set
Context readme  rev 1
  Name: VS Code typing
  Connections: none

$ dbgjs process attach 35668 --set
Attachment: created
Target renderer-1  [running]  readme/process-tree-33216  gen 1  rev 3
  Pause: none

$ dbgjs target eval document.title
readme-demo - Visual Studio Code
````

## Open an editor with real keyboard input

Playwright clicks the workbench, presses Ctrl+N, and waits for the new editor.

````console
$ dbgjs playwright 'await page.locator(".monaco-workbench").click();
await page.keyboard.press("Control+n");
await page.locator(".editor-group-container .monaco-editor").waitFor();
return await page.title();'
"Untitled-1 - readme-demo - Visual Studio Code"
````

## Measure the first edit

Start precise coverage and capture a baseline. Type into the editor and save
the next capture. Exclude the baseline when viewing it, without modifying the
stored capture.

````console
$ dbgjs coverage start
Coverage recording started.

$ dbgjs coverage capture --id background
Captured background.

$ dbgjs target type 'hello from dbgjs'

$ dbgjs coverage stop --id typing
````

## Run JavaScript against the discovered object

Resolve the heap instance ID to a live object using
`HeapProfiler.getObjectByHeapObjectId`. Pass the returned remote `objectId` to
`Runtime.callFunctionOn`; `this` is the actual `PieceTreeTextBuffer` instance,
not a copy of the snapshot data. Its methods return the text typed earlier.

````console
$ dbgjs target cdp HeapProfiler.getObjectByHeapObjectId --params '{"objectId":"3151931","objectGroup":"readme-heap"}'
{
  "result": {
    "type": "object",
    "className": "s",
    "description": "s",
    "objectId": "5915318683987910857.1.167"
  }
}

$ dbgjs target cdp Runtime.callFunctionOn --params '{"objectId":"5915318683987910857.1.167","functionDeclaration":"function () { return { lineCount: this.getLineCount(), firstLine: this.getLineContent(1).slice(0, 17) }; }","returnByValue":true}'
{
  "result": {
    "type": "object",
    "value": {
      "lineCount": 1,
      "firstLine": "hello from dbgjs!"
    }
  }
}
````

The instance is selected from the buffer IDs printed above. Replay verifies
its line count and text prefix, then releases the temporary remote object
group. This step requires the same live target and a surviving object; the
stored snapshot remains useful offline, but cannot run code on its own.
